body:
Why different Buddhist buildings were needed

A Buddhist monastic complex could contain buildings serving different purposes. A stupa provided a sacred monument for veneration, a hall created space for collective worship, and residential buildings accommodated monks. These needs produced distinct forms of architecture.

Chaitya-griha: A Buddhist prayer or worship hall, often containing a stupa at its far end.
Vihara: A monastery or monastic residence, commonly organised with individual cells around a shared space.

The word chaitya has a broader historical meaning and could refer to a sacred place or shrine. In architectural descriptions of Buddhist caves, the more precise term chaitya hall identifies the enclosed worship space.

The plan of a chaitya hall

Many early Buddhist chaitya halls were elongated structures ending in a rounded or apsidal rear. A stupa stood at this curved end. Pillars could divide the hall into a central nave and side aisles, allowing movement around the stupa.

The roof often imitated a vaulted form associated with earlier timber architecture. At the entrance, a large horseshoe-shaped opening, known as a chaitya arch, could admit light into the interior. This motif is also called a gavaksha in architectural description.

The exact plan varied by site and period. Some halls lacked an elaborate columned interior, while later examples introduced prominent Buddha images and more extensive sculpture.

The plan of a vihara

A typical early vihara contained a central hall with small cells arranged around it. A verandah might extend across the entrance. The cells provided spaces for monastic residence, while the hall served the needs of the community.

As Buddhist religious practices and architecture developed, some larger viharas acquired a shrine containing an image of the Buddha on the rear wall. Therefore, identifying a building as a vihara does not mean that it could never contain a shrine.

Rock-cut and structural construction

Rock-cut architecture is created by removing material from an existing rock mass to produce rooms, halls, pillars and sculptural details. In contrast, structural architecture is built by assembling materials such as brick, stone or timber.

A rock-cut chaitya hall may imitate the plan and roof form of a timber-built or structural hall. The presence of a curved roof shape does not, by itself, establish that a building was originally made of timber; it may be a later imitation carved into stone.

Both worship halls and monasteries could be constructed as free-standing buildings or excavated as caves. The distinction between chaitya and vihara therefore concerns their principal function and layout, not merely the material used.

Important examples

Karla, also spelled Karle, is especially associated with a large rock-cut Buddhist chaitya hall. Bhaja preserves early examples of Buddhist cave architecture. At Ajanta, Caves 9 and 10 are important early chaitya halls, while Caves 19 and 26 illustrate later developments with more elaborate sculptural decoration.

Examples of early vihara caves include Ajanta Cave 12. Later monasteries could have larger halls, more elaborate facades and dedicated Buddha shrines.

Prelims focus

  • A chaitya-griha is principally a worship hall.
  • A vihara is principally a monastic residence.
  • Early chaitya halls often had an apsidal end containing a stupa.
  • Karla is a major example of a rock-cut chaitya hall.
  • Ajanta Caves 9 and 10 are early chaitya halls.
  • Trap: A cave is a construction method, not a building function; both chaityas and viharas can be rock-cut.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, pp. 35–41; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 105–107; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, pp. 122–126.]

pictures.alt: Plans compare an elongated chaitya with a stupa at its rounded rear and an early vihara with monastic cells around a central hall.
pictures.caption: The principal differences between a chaitya hall and an early vihara.

title: Chaitya Halls and Viharas: Buddhist Spaces for Worship and Monastic Life

body:
The development of rock-cut architecture

Rock-cut architecture developed into a major form of Indian sacred construction because a hillside or rock face could be excavated to create an enclosed space. Unlike a structural building assembled from separate materials, a cave hall was carved from the rock itself.

Some of the earliest surviving monumental rock-cut caves are at Barabar in Bihar, dating to the 3rd century BCE. They are associated with Mauryan patronage under Ashoka and with the Ajivika sect. The entrance to the Lomas Rishi cave is especially noted for its early chaitya-arch form.

Barabar is a chronological landmark in Indian rock-cut architecture, but its early Mauryan caves were associated with the Ajivikas. They should not be incorrectly classified as Buddhist monasteries merely because later Buddhist halls used related architectural forms.

Western Indian Buddhist cave sites

Western India contains numerous Buddhist cave complexes, especially in present-day Maharashtra. Important examples include Bhaja, Karla, Nashik, Kanheri and Ajanta. Their plans include chaitya halls, viharas and later combinations of residential and shrine spaces.

Ajanta is especially important for understanding both the early and later development of Buddhist caves. Its earliest monuments date to approximately the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, while major later excavations and decoration belong broadly to the 5th and 6th centuries CE.

The site contains early chaitya halls such as Caves 9 and 10 and later examples such as Caves 19 and 26. Many other caves were used as viharas. The surviving paintings depict Buddhist subjects, including Jataka narratives, while sculptural programmes became increasingly elaborate in later phases.

Ellora and the coexistence of religious traditions

Ellora in Maharashtra is a major rock-cut complex containing monuments associated with Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism. Its 34 numbered caves are commonly grouped as follows:

Ellora cavesPrincipal religious associationImportant distinction
1–12BuddhistMonastic and worship spaces
13–29HinduIncludes the Kailasa temple at Cave 16
30–34JainRock-cut Jain shrines and sculpture

Cave 16 at Ellora is the monumental Kailasa temple, associated with Shiva. It is a rock-cut temple, not a Buddhist chaitya or Jain shrine. The distinction is important because the presence of 3 religious traditions at Ellora does not make every cave a Buddhist monument.

Structural Buddhist architecture: Mahabodhi and Nalanda

Not all major Buddhist buildings were caves. The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya, Bihar, is an important structural brick temple associated with the Buddha's enlightenment. Its first shrine is traditionally linked with Ashoka, while the main surviving temple form dates primarily to the 5th–6th centuries CE, with later repairs and restoration. It shows how Buddhist worship could be centred on a structural shrine rather than only a stupa mound or excavated cave.

Nalanda Mahavihara in Bihar developed into a major residential and educational Buddhist establishment. Its archaeological remains include viharas, shrines, stupas and other structures. The term mahavihara describes a large monastic establishment, not merely a single monk's cell. Nalanda's architectural development demonstrates how residential buildings, teaching activities and sacred spaces could form one extensive complex.

Gujarat connection: Devni Mori

Devni Mori, near Shamlaji in the present-day Arvalli district of Gujarat, is an important archaeological example of Buddhist architecture in the state. Excavations revealed a brick stupa, monastic remains and a relic casket bearing an inscription. The discovery demonstrates that Buddhist architectural activity extended into northern Gujarat.

The site is associated with the early centuries CE, particularly the 4th-century CE phase of its substantial Buddhist remains. The combination of a stupa and monasteries makes Devni Mori especially useful for understanding how a religious complex could integrate relic veneration and monastic residence.

Prelims focus

  • Barabar caves in Bihar were associated with the Ajivikas under Mauryan patronage.
  • Ajanta is a major Buddhist cave complex in Maharashtra.
  • Ellora contains Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monuments.
  • Ellora Cave 16 is the Hindu Kailasa temple.
  • Mahabodhi is a major structural brick Buddhist temple; Nalanda is a mahavihara.
  • Devni Mori near Shamlaji is an important Buddhist archaeological site in Gujarat.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapters 3–4 and 6, pp. 20–21, 35–45 and 90–93; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ajanta Caves, Description; Ellora Caves, Description; Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya, Brief Synthesis; Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara, Brief Synthesis, all consulted 23 November 2026; Arvalli District Administration, Government of Gujarat, Devni Mori, site description, consulted 23 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India material reproduced by Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Buddhist Monuments, section Devnimori.]

pictures.alt: Barabar, Ajanta and Ellora are rock-cut sites; Mahabodhi is a brick temple, Nalanda a mahavihara, and Devni Mori has a brick stupa and monastic remains.
pictures.caption: Recognising major Buddhist architectural sites by their characteristic forms.

title: Buddhist Caves, Brick Temples and Monastic Centres Across India

body:
The religious foundation of Jain architecture

Jain sacred architecture is closely connected with the veneration of the Tirthankaras, revered spiritual teachers who show the path towards liberation. Jain tradition recognises 24 Tirthankaras in the present cycle. Rishabhanatha, also called Adinatha, is the 1st; Parshvanatha is the 23rd; and Mahavira is the 24th.

Architecture provides space for devotion, contemplation and monastic life. Jain traditions produced both rock-cut monuments and structural temples. Their appearance may share regional construction practices with Buddhist or Hindu buildings, but the sacred images and religious associations distinguish them.

Udayagiri and Khandagiri in Odisha

The Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves, near Bhubaneswar in Odisha, are prominent examples of early Jain rock-cut architecture. They contain monastic cells, pillared verandahs and carved entrances. Some caves have more elaborate facades and sculptural decoration.

These caves are associated with the period of Kharavela, a ruler of Kalinga whose inscriptions provide important historical evidence. The Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri is associated with him. The complex is therefore important for connecting Jain monastic architecture with recorded political patronage.

The cells were not identical to large congregational halls. They provided spaces for monks, while the more elaborate facades and shared areas demonstrate how a monastic complex could combine residential and symbolic functions.

Jain caves at Ellora

The later Jain excavations at Ellora are principally Caves 30–34. Their architecture includes excavated shrines, pillars, halls and detailed sculptural representations of Jain sacred figures.

The Jain caves belong to a different phase and religious tradition from Ellora's early Buddhist caves. Their presence demonstrates that rock-cut architecture was not restricted to one religion.

How Tirthankara images are recognised

Jain Tirthankaras are frequently represented in restrained meditative postures. Two important forms are padmasana, a seated cross-legged posture, and kayotsarga, an upright standing meditation posture.

Because several Tirthankara images may have similar bodily positions and facial expressions, lanchhanas, or identifying emblems, are especially important. They are commonly represented on the pedestal or associated with the image.

TirthankaraNumberCommon identifying emblem
Rishabhanatha or Adinatha1Bull
Ajitanatha2Elephant
Neminatha22Conch
Parshvanatha23Serpent
Mahavira24Lion

Parshvanatha is especially recognisable in many sculptures by a serpent-hood canopy above the head. Neminatha may be identified by the conch emblem on the pedestal. However, not every early Jain image carries the complete set of identifying symbols familiar from later traditions. Damaged or incomplete sculptures may require inscriptional or contextual evidence for reliable identification.

Jain and Buddhist images: an important distinction

A seated meditating figure is not automatically the Buddha. Buddhist images may be identified through mudras, bodily attributes, associated stories and accompanying figures. Jain Tirthankara images are identified through their own iconographic conventions, including lanchhanas, meditation postures and associated attendants.

Architecture and iconography must be read together. A carved religious figure should not be assigned to Buddhism or Jainism solely because it is seated in meditation.

Prelims focus

  • Jain tradition recognises 24 Tirthankaras.
  • Udayagiri and Khandagiri in Odisha contain early Jain rock-cut caves.
  • Kharavela is associated with the Hathigumpha inscription.
  • Ellora Caves 30–34 are Jain caves.
  • Neminatha's emblem is the conch; Parshvanatha's is the serpent.
  • Trap: A meditating human figure does not by itself prove whether an image represents the Buddha or a Jain Tirthankara.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 88–89; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapters 4 and 6, pp. 41–45 and 93–95; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ellora Caves, Description, consulted 23 November 2026; National Museum, New Delhi, Indian Museum Collections, Western India, Neminatha entry; Metropolitan Museum of Art, Standing Jain Tirthankara Parshvanatha, collection entry, consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Jain Architecture: Rock-cut Monasteries, Tirthankara Images and Sacred Symbols
